description: We are doing our best effort to make a contribution scale product with real impact through team effort and workmanship.
summary: We built the Burning Activity Calendar, a web app that turns 27 years of NASA FIRMS satellite fire detections into one consistent record for Pakistan, from 2000 to yesterday. NASA's two fire sensors disagree: for the same fires, MODIS (since 2000, 1 km pixels) records about 27 fire-days where VIIRS (since 2012, 375 m) records 100. Simply joining them creates a fake jump in fire activity in 2012. On top of that, VIIRS on Suomi NPP stopped delivering data on 2 November 2026. Our method converts MODIS and NOAA-20 counts into VIIRS S-NPP units, separately for every 1° block and every month, using only days when both sensors observed. Tested on years the method never saw, the error falls from about 73% to under 1%, and the NOAA-20 hand-over stays within 2%. The app shows when and where Pakistan burns, how unusual each month is, and how this week compares with every year since 2000. This matters because crop burning drives the November smog season in Punjab, and decisions need fair comparisons with the past.
details:
What it does

The Burning Activity Calendar answers two questions for any area of Pakistan: when does it burn, and is this season unusual? You can choose all of Pakistan, a province, any of 134 districts, or draw your own area on the map. The app then shows:

a burning calendar of years against months or weeks, where the May wheat and October–November rice burning seasons stand out at a glance;

an anomaly view showing how unusual each month was compared with 2001–2020;

"Now vs the past": this week and this year so far, ranked against every year since 2000. For example, 5–11 Nov 2026 is the 3rd highest of 27 years, 2.8× the 2001–2011 average;

critical weeks (how often each week is among the 10 busiest of its year), season start, peak and end dates, the long-term trend per decade, and the typical year;

a sensor comparison chart and a validation table inside the app, so anyone can check our claims.

How it works

Clean: we keep vegetation fires only, removing FIRMS-labelled industrial sources and low-confidence detections. Near-real-time data has no type label, so we remove detections at locations FIRMS flagged as industrial in the archive. Checked against FIRMS' own labels, this catches 97.8% of industrial sources and wrongly removes 1.65% of vegetation fires.

Count: we count "fire-days" on a 0.1° grid (about 11 km, 8,206 cells across Pakistan). A cell scores one fire-day on any day with at least one detection. This is fairer than counting raw points, because a high-resolution sensor can record several points for one fire.

Calibrate: for each 1° block and calendar month, we compare MODIS and VIIRS S-NPP fire-days on days when both delivered data. Blocks with few fires are pulled towards the national monthly ratio, so one noisy ratio can't distort a region.

Harmonize: the final record is MODIS converted to S-NPP units for 2000–2011, real S-NPP counts from 2012 to 2 Nov 2026, and NOAA-20 converted to S-NPP units afterwards.

Validate: all tests use years the method never saw.

MODIS to S-NPP, tested on 2023–2025: bias −0.1% (−72.8% uncorrected), R² 0.937.

Backwards in time, tested on 2012–2014: +0.6%.

NOAA-20 to S-NPP, tested on 2024–2025: +1.1%, R² 0.996.

Live test on 2026: +2.0%, R² 0.995.

Benefits and intended impact

FIRMS shows where fires are right now. Our app adds the long-term context: whether a season is earlier, longer or more intense than usual, measured with one consistent scale across 27 years. This can help environmental agencies, researchers and land managers time crop-residue enforcement and smog warnings, target districts with recurring problems, and judge whether policies are working. The data refreshes daily from the FIRMS API.

Tools and technologies

Data: NASA FIRMS (MODIS Collection 6.1; VIIRS 375 m from Suomi NPP and NOAA-20), using the yearly archives and the FIRMS API for the current year. Province and district boundaries come from geoBoundaries.

Backend: Python, FastAPI and DuckDB (a fast single-file analytical database), with NumPy and Shapely.

Frontend: Next.js (TypeScript), Tailwind CSS, MapLibre GL for the map and Apache ECharts for the charts.

Hosting: Render (API) and Vercel (website), both on free tiers, plus a GitHub Actions workflow for the daily data refresh.

What makes it creative

Instead of a black-box model, we use a transparent, checkable ratio method calibrated per region and per month. It converts totals rather than inventing individual fires.

We handled a real sensor change that happened during the challenge, the end of S-NPP delivery on 2 Nov 2026, by carrying the record over to NOAA-20 with the same method and testing it live.

The calendar format makes a 27-year satellite record readable for non-specialists in seconds.

Validation is part of the product, not hidden in a report.

Factors we considered

Fairness of comparison: we chose the fire-day unit, compared only days when both sensors observed, and pulled noisy regional ratios towards the national value.

Honesty about limits: near-real-time data can change slightly when NASA's final version replaces it; clouds hide fires from both sensors; the 11 km grid compares activity, not individual fires.

Scope: we focused on Pakistan for local relevance and to fit free hosting. The method works for any country.

Cost and access: the app is free to use with no login, open source, and runs entirely on free infrastructure.

Live app: https://burning-activity-calendar.vercel.app

Yearly VIIRS (S-NPP satellite) data for Pakistan
Yearly VIIRS (VIIRS NOAA-20) data for Pakistan
NASA FIRMS live API (current year) and 2026 data for all three sensors: science-quality where it exists, then near-real-time up to 13 November.
projectRefs: geoBoundaries (province and district borders), open-data administrative boundaries for Pakistan. ADM1 = provinces, ADM2 = districts; 134 regions in total. Also used to cut the live API data to Pakistan's border.
CARTO Dark Matter basemap (display only), the dark background map with countries, cities and labels. It contains no fire data and isn't used in any calculation.
